title: Sapiens
author: Yuval Noah Harari
blurb: Sapiens tells the story of our species, from an insignificant African ape to the ruler of the planet. Harari organises this history around three big turning points. The Cognitive Revolution, about 70,000 years ago, gave Sapiens the ability to believe in shared stories, letting strangers cooperate in huge numbers. The Agricultural Revolution, around 12,000 years ago, multiplied our numbers but often made individual lives harder. The Scientific Revolution, beginning about 500 years ago, unleashed unprecedented power by admitting ignorance and investing in discovery. Along the way, Harari shows how money, empires and religions gradually unified humankind into one global society. He asks an uncomfortable question: has all this progress actually made us happier? The book ends by considering how biotechnology may soon let Sapiens redesign itself, and what we should want to become.

lessons.t: We Were Once One Human Among Many
lessons.b: Homo sapiens once shared the Earth with other human species such as Neanderthals, and we are the only ones left.
Sapiens came to dominate because we can believe in shared fictions like gods, nations and companies, which let huge numbers of strangers cooperate.

lessons.b: Ancient hunter-gatherers often enjoyed varied diets, broad skills and fewer working hours than the farmers who came after them.
The Agricultural Revolution produced more food and more people, but for most individuals it meant harder work, poorer diets and new diseases.
Laws, hierarchies and rights exist because many people believe in them, and writing helped these imagined orders grow far beyond village size.

lessons.t: Money: The Most Universal Trust System
lessons.b: Money works not because of what it is made of, but because everyone trusts that everyone else will accept it.

lessons.t: Empires and Religions Unify the World
lessons.b: Empires and universal religions, often through violence and conquest, steadily merged countless small cultures into ever larger shared ones.
The Scientific Revolution began when people admitted how much they did not know and started investing in finding out.

lessons.t: Credit, Capitalism and Faith in Tomorrow
lessons.b: Modern economies grow because people trust that the future will be richer, which lets them lend and invest in science, exploration and business.
